formula: los ~ procedure + sex + admit + (1 | hospital)
notes: Read azpro.Rd: 1991 Arizona Medpar cardiovascular patients (CABG or PTCA), los the length of stay, hospital the encrypted facility code. The help example fits glm(los ~ procedure + sex + admit, family=poisson) (Hilbe, Negative Binomial Regression 2011) and comments out glm.nb; no source fits hospital, so the patients-within-hospitals design is rendered as a random intercept. age75 is a usable covariate the example leaves out. The same table as COUNT azprocedure, its columns in another order.

formula: los ~ procedure + sex + admit + (1 | hospital)
notes: Read azprocedure.Rd: the same 1991 Arizona Medpar patients and columns as COUNT azpro (Hilbe, Modeling Count Data 2014; Negative Binomial Regression 2011), hospital the encrypted facility code. The help example fits glm(los ~ procedure + sex + admit, family=poisson), msme's nbinomial and MASS's glm.nb; no source fits hospital, so the patients-within-hospitals design is rendered as a random intercept. age75 is a usable covariate the example leaves out.

formula: los ~ hmo + white + type2 + type3 + (1 | provnum)
notes: Read medpar.Rd (1991 Arizona Medpar, DRG 112, provnum the provider id) and the book code the package ships. inst/HILBE_SCRIPTS/HILBE-MCD-Rcode.r, Table 9.9 (Hilbe, Modeling Count Data 2014, section 9.6.2, Random Intercept Poisson): gamlssNP(los ~ hmo + white + type2 + type3, random=~1|provnum, data=medpar, family=PO, mixture=gq, K=20), a normal random intercept by Gaussian quadrature; Table 9.8 fits the same terms plus age80 by GEE with id=medpar$provnum. inst/HILBE_NBR2_FIGURES/hilbe.NBR2.F14.1.r (Negative Binomial Regression 2nd ed., Figure 14.1) fits the same model with family=NBI, the negative binomial variant of the same response and grouping, so no second row. type is the categorical coding of the dummies type1 to type3 (type1 the baseline), both ignored. died and age80 are usable columns.

formula: docvis ~ outwork + female + age + factor(edlevel) + (1 | id)
notes: Read rwm5yr.Rd: German health registry panel 1984 to 1988 (Hilbe and Greene 2008), id the patient id and year the wave. The help example fits pooled glm(docvis ~ outwork + female + age + factor(edlevel), family=poisson) and, in dontrun, nbinomial and glm.nb; the Modeling Count Data code the package ships (inst/HILBE_SCRIPTS/HILBE-MCD-Rcode.r) uses only its 1984 wave (rwm1984 <- subset(rwm5yr, year==1984)) in GLMs. A panel fitted only pooled, so id is rendered as a random intercept (panel ruling). hospvis is the alternate response; edlevel1 to edlevel4 are the dummies of edlevel. year, married, kids, hhninc, educ and self are usable columns. Negative Binomial Regression 2nd ed. chapter 14 (count panel models) was not at hand to check for a random-effects fit on these data.

formula: accident ~ op + co.70.74 + co.75.79 + offset(log(service)) + (1 | ship)
notes: Read ships.Rd (McCullagh and Nelder 1989; Hardin and Hilbe): accidents per ship, construction and operation period, log(service) the offset; the page says ship can be used as a panel identifier. The help fits glm and glm.nb and, in dontrun, gee(accident ~ op + co.70.74 + co.75.79 + offset(log(service)), family=poisson, corstr=exchangeable, id=ship), so the cluster is rendered as a random intercept; GEE is no mixed model, so published_model no. Stata's xtpoisson manual fits the same data with a ship random effect (stata_ships, in the registry). co.65.69 is a dummy the example leaves out; a ship-period never operated has no accident and no service.

formula: cbind(npos, nneg) ~ treatment + (1 | clinic)
notes: Read clinics.Rd (toy data set for binomial response, Booth and Hobert 1998; eight clinics by two treatments as built on the page) and the example in get_cPredVar.Rd: HLfit(cbind(npos,nneg)~treatment+(1|clinic), family=binomial(), data=clinics), a logit-normal GLMM with a clinic random intercept, repeated in tests/testthat/test-predVar.R; betabin.Rd fits cbind(npos,nneg)~1+(1|clinic) with family betabin(). Successes stored beside their failures without a trials column are count (faraway soybean ruling), so npos is the response and nneg is ignored; the source's family is binomial with npos + nneg trials.

formula: y ~ crack0 + (1 | specimen); rand.family = inverse.Gamma(log); resid.model = ~ cycle + (1 | specimen)
notes: crack has no help page (spaMM-internal.Rd: not documented but used in an example). The example in phi-resid.model.Rd, citing Lee, Nelder and Pawitan (2006) chapter 11: HLfit(y~crack0+(1|specimen), family=Gamma(log), data=crack, rand.family=inverse.Gamma(log), resid.model=list(formula=~cycle+(1|specimen))), a double HGLM; tests/testthat/test-dhglm.R fits the same with HLmethod=REML. RULE GAP: the specimen effect of the mean is inverse-gamma on the log scale, not Gaussian, and a second specimen effect enters the dispersion model; both are named in the formula. cycle enters only the dispersion model. The columns are undocumented.

formula: Mate ~ TypeF + TypeM + TypeF:TypeM + (1 | Female) + (1 | Male)
notes: Read salamander.Rd (McCullagh and Nelder 1989 ch. 14; Arnold et al. 1996; borrowed from HGLMMM): example HLfit(cbind(Mate,1-Mate)~TypeF+TypeM+TypeF*TypeM+(1|Female)+(1|Male), family=binomial(), data=salamander, method=ML), crossed female and male random intercepts on a binary Mate. The package page (spaMM.Rd) also fits intercept-only variants with a Beta(logit) male effect and with males nested in females. Cross is the TypeF by TypeM combination, ignored; Season and Experiment are design columns no example fits. As lme4's copy notes, female and male ids may repeat across the three experiments; the example treats the ids as the groups.

formula: y ~ X1 + X2 + X1*X3 + X2*X3 + I(X2^2) + (1 | batch); resid.model = ~ X3 + I(X3^2)
notes: Read wafers.Rd (Robinson et al. 2006; Lee et al. 2011: resistivity of wafers, batch the day, the one random effect) and the example in HLfit.Rd: HLfit(y ~ X1+X2+X1*X3+X2*X3+I(X2^2)+(1|batch), family=Gamma(log), resid.model = ~ X3+I(X3^2), data=wafers), a Gamma GLMM with log link and a structured dispersion; the same page refits it with an inverse-Gamma batch effect. Other examples fit simplifications (y ~ 1+(1|batch)) and a random-slope variant y~X1+(X2|batch) of the same response and grouping. I(X2^2) is a derived term in the formula only.

formula: y ~ Subject + TchExp + Stu.Tch + (1 | School) + (1 | Zip)
notes: Read the ohio help page: ohioGrades is the derived dataset for analyzing the percentage passed based on Zip codes, y the percentage passed in each school for five subjects (Subject), TchExp and Stu.Tch school covariates, School the school index and Zip its zip code; ohioZipDistMat, built from its Zip, is the spatial distance matrix for a zip-level effect. Neither hglm.Rd, hglm2.Rd, the hglm vignette nor Alam, Ronnegard and Shen (2015, R Journal 7(2)) fits it, so the model is proposed: school intercepts over the five subject rows of each school, and zip intercepts. RULE GAP: the page calls it derived from ohioSchools, whose subject columns V26 to V30 it stacks long beside covariates computed from ohioSchools; filed as the long form, which the registry holds for a wide table.

formula: V23 ~ 1 + (1 | V5); rand.family = CAR(D = ohioDistrictDistMat)
notes: Read the ohio help page (LeSage and Pace 2009 web data; col 23 the median of 4th grade prof scores, col 5 the district irn) and Alam, Ronnegard and Shen (2015, R Journal 7(2), section Ohio elementary school grades data set): We regress the median of 4th grade proficiency scores, y, on an intercept, based on school districts, y_ij = mu + v_j + e_ij with v CAR-distributed over adjacent districts, fitted as hglm(y = ohioMedian$MedianScore, X = X, Z = model.matrix(~ 0 + district), rand.family = CAR(D = ohioDistrictDistMat)); hglm.Rd fits the same as hglm(fixed = MedianScore ~ 1, random = ~ 1 | district, rand.family = CAR(D = ohioDistrictDistMat), data = ohioMedian). RULE GAP: the model is documented on ohioMedian, the derived subset of this table (MedianScore is V23 and district is V5 without its last digit, as the first rows show) for the 1,860 schools the paper matched to a census district; filed on this superset, ohioMedian excluded as derived. V1 (zip), V2 and V3 (zip centroid coordinates), V4 and V21 (building ids) are ids or coordinates; V22 and V26 to V30 are alternate responses.

formula: Mate ~ TypeF + TypeM + TypeF:TypeM + (1 | Female) + (1 | Male)
notes: Read the hglm.data help page (McCullagh and Nelder 1989, section 14.5): no example, and neither hglm.Rd, hglm2.Rd nor the hglm vignette fits it. The model is recalled from the cited section, the salamander mating experiment with crossed random effects for females and males on the logit scale, as lme4's and spaMM's copies fit it. Cross is the TypeF by TypeM combination, ignored; Season and Experiment are design columns. Female and male ids may repeat across the three experiments.

formula: y ~ x1 + x3 + x5 + x6 + (1 | Device); disp = ~ x2 + x3
notes: Read the hglm.data help page (GenStat; Lee, Nelder and Pawitan 2006; Myers, Montgomery and Vining 2002): a 2^(6-2) factorial, camber y measured on each substrate Device. hglm.Rd and hglm2.Rd of the hglm package, which uses hglm.data's tables: m11 <- hglm(fixed = y ~ x1 + x3 + x5 + x6, random = ~ 1|Device, family = Gamma(link = log), disp = ~ x2 + x3, data = semiconductor), a Gamma HGLM with a dispersion model, refitted as hglm2(y ~ x1 + x3 + x5 + x6 + (1|Device), family = Gamma(link = log), disp = ~ x2 + x3) and with Z = kronecker(diag(16), rep(1, 4)). x2 enters only the dispersion model, x4 no model.

formula: tarsus ~ sex + (1 | dam) + (1 | fosternest)
documented_prior: prior = list(R = list(V = 1, nu = 0.002), G = list(G1 = list(V = 1, nu = 0.002), G2 = list(V = 1, nu = 0.002)))
notes: Read BTdata.Rd (Hadfield et al. 2007) and the course notes of MCMCglmm 2.29 (vignettes/Lecture3.tex, chapter Categorical Random Interactions; the vignettes left the CRAN package after 2.29): m3a.1 <- MCMCglmm(tarsus ~ sex, random = ~dam + fosternest, data = BTdata, prior = prior), dam the genetic mother and fosternest the nest of rearing, crossed by the brood swap. Later models of the chapter let the dam variance differ by sex (idh(sex):dam, us(sex):dam). The Overview vignette (Hadfield 2010) fits tarsus and back jointly with an animal-model pedigree term and fosternest (row 2 files its back part; its tarsus part shares row 1's response). Chapter 8 (Lecture8.tex) fits sex ~ 1 with a dam effect, family categorical after setting UNK to missing; not filed since sex holds three values. animal is the chick id, one row each; back is the other response.

formula: back ~ sex + hatchdate + (1 | gr(animal, cov = A)) + (1 | fosternest)
documented_prior: prior = list(R = list(V = 1/3, n = 2), G = list(G1 = list(V = 1/3, n = 2), G2 = list(V = 1/3, n = 2)))
notes: Overview vignette of MCMCglmm 2.29 (Hadfield 2010, section Software): m1 <- MCMCglmm(cbind(tarsus, back) ~ trait:sex + trait:hatchdate - 1, random = ~ us(trait):animal + us(trait):fosternest, rcov = ~ us(trait):units, prior = prior, family = rep(gaussian, 2), data = BTdata, pedigree = BTped), prior V = diag(2)/3 and n = 2 for R, G1 and G2, trimmed here to back. The animal effect is the additive genetic effect, correlated through the relationship matrix A of the pedigree BTped; animal has one row per chick, so it is no grouping factor (ignored, its term kept in the formula). The page notes that the family structure could be fitted more efficiently as a dam effect; dam is ignored here since this model carries it through A. tarsus is the other response.

formula: PO ~ 1 + (1 | FSfamily)
notes: Read PlodiaPO.Rd (phenoloxidase of Indian meal moth caterpillars by full-sib family and plate, PO Box-Cox transformed with power 0.141; Tidbury and Boots 2007) and MCMCglmm.Rd example 1, univariate Gaussian model with standard random effect: MCMCglmm(PO~1, random=~FSfamily, data=PlodiaPO), the package default prior. plate is a blocking column no example fits.

formula: Pupated ~ 1 + (1 | FSfamily); residual (units) variance fixed at 1
documented_prior: prior.m2b.1 = list(R = list(V = 1, fix = 1), G = list(G1 = list(V = 1, nu = 0.002)))
notes: Read PlodiaRB.Rd (resistance of Indian meal moth caterpillars to the granulosis virus as a binary trait per individual, PlodiaR's family totals expanded) and the course notes of MCMCglmm 2.29 (vignettes/Lecture2.tex, binary data): m2b.1 <- MCMCglmm(Pupated ~ 1, random = ~FSfamily, family = categorical, data = PlodiaRB, prior = prior.m2b.1), a logit model with the residual variance fixed at 1, refitted as m2b.2 with it fixed at 2 to show the dependence on that choice. date_laid and date_Ass are family-level dates no model fits.

formula: dbh.cm ~ SSasympOrig(age.bh, asymptote, scale), asymptotic regression through the origin; tree-specific asymptote and scale (fixed and random = asymptote + scale ~ 1 | tree.ID); correlation = corARMA(p = 1, q = 2)
notes: NONLINEAR: read gutten.Rd (von Guttenberg 1915 Norway spruce stem analyses; Robinson and Hamann 2010) and the book code the package ships, inst/resources/scripts/book/fitting_models.r: gutten.d <- groupedData(dbh.cm ~ age.bh | tree.ID), gutten.nlme.0 <- nlme(nlsList(dbh.cm ~ SSasympOrig(age.bh, asymptote, scale))) with fixed and random asymptote + scale ~ 1, then gutten.nlme.1 <- update(gutten.nlme.0, correlation = corARMA(p = 1, q = 2)), whose intervals the chapter reports; gutten.nlme.2 tries SSasymp with three parameters, and a try() lets scale depend on site. The book drops rows without dbh.cm. tree is the tree number within location, which tree.ID combines; height, volume and age.base are alternate responses and an alternate age; site and location are tree-level columns no model keeps.

formula: height.m ~ dbhib.cm + I(dbhib.cm^2) + (1 | Forest.ID) + (dbhib.cm | Tree.ID); correlation = corCAR1()
notes: Read stage.Rd (Stage 1963 grand fir stem analyses, decadal heights and diameters of trees from national forests; Robinson and Hamann 2010) and the book code the package ships, inst/resources/scripts/book/fitting_models.r: the height-diameter models build from hd.lme.1 (random = ~1 | Forest.ID, Decade 0 only) and hd.lme.3 (random = ~1 | Forest.ID/Tree.ID) to hd.lme.4 <- lme(height.m ~ dbhib.cm + I(dbhib.cm^2), random = list(~ 1 | Forest.ID, ~ dbhib.cm | Tree.ID)) and the final hd.lme.5 <- update(hd.lme.4, correlation = corCAR1()), continuous-time autocorrelation within tree. age.lme.1 (Age ~ dbhib.cm, random = ~1 | Forest.ID/Tree.ID) serves an added-variable plot only. Forest, HabType, Dbhib and Height are the integer codes and imperial units of Forest.ID, Hab.ID, dbhib.cm and height.m. I(dbhib.cm^2) is a derived term in the formula only; Decade, Age and Hab.ID are usable columns.

formula: log(vol.m3) ~ log(dbh.cm) + (1 | plot)
notes: Read sweetgum.Rd (Lenhart's sweetgum trees from Texas, one row per felled tree, plot the plot it was felled in, vol.m3 integrated from a spline over the stem measures; Robinson and Hamann 2010 section 2.4.2) and the book code the package ships (inst/resources/scripts/book/regression.r): sweetgum.lm.ld <- lm(log.vol.m3 ~ log.dbh.cm), trees treated as independent, so the plot design is rendered as a random intercept. tree is the tree id; dbh.in and height.ft are the imperial copies of dbh.cm and height.m; stump.ht.ft and height.m are usable columns.

formula: log(height.m) ~ dbh.cm * species + (1 | plot)
notes: Read ufc.Rd (Upper Flat Creek forest cruise 1991, trees measured on variable radius plots; Robinson and Hamann 2010) and the book code the package ships (inst/resources/scripts/book/regression.r): hd.lm.1 <- lm(I(log(height.m)) ~ dbh.cm * species, subset = height.m > 0) and the weighted hd.lm.5 <- lm(height.m ~ dbh.cm * species, weights = dbh.cm^-2), trees treated as independent; ufc.r sums the trees to their sample point. The trees-within-plots design is rendered as a plot random intercept. tree is the tree label within plot.
